```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 120, out.width = "100%", raster3d = 1e5, dev = "svglite", fig.ext = "svg",
  dev.args = list(pointsize = 14))
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 17) + theme(
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.key = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.box.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA)))
```

A symmetric tensor is a matrix whose eigenvectors give three perpendicular directions and whose eigenvalues give their magnitudes. `geom_tensor_3d()` draws one tensor at each position. It accepts symmetric positive semidefinite matrices in a list-column.

```{r tensors}
d <- data.frame(x = c(0, 3, 6), y = 0, z = 0,
                shape = c("Linear", "Planar", "Isotropic"))
d$tensor <- list(diag(c(1, 0.25, 0.25)), diag(c(1, 1, 0.25)), diag(3))
ggplot(d, aes(x, y, z = z, tensor = tensor, fill = shape)) +
  geom_tensor_3d(glyph = "superquadric", gamma = 3, detail = 2) +
  coord_3d(aspect = "data") + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Kindlmann's superquadric construction uses the relative linear and planar anisotropy of each tensor to choose its surface shape. `gamma` controls edge sharpness. `glyph = "ellipsoid"` uses a sphere stretched along the tensor eigenvectors. `gamma = 0` produces the same surface shape for a superquadric.

The three semi-axis lengths equal `scale` times the eigenvalues, in scale-transformed position units. A covariance ellipsoid uses the square roots of covariance eigenvalues; `geom_ellipsoid_3d(aes(sigma = covariance))` draws that geometry directly. `stat_ellipsoid_3d()` estimates covariance regions from groups of observations.

## Rotated tensors

Multiplying a diagonal matrix on the left by a rotation and on the right by its transpose gives the tensor in the plotting coordinates.

```{r rotated}
angle <- pi / 4
rotation <- matrix(c(cos(angle), sin(angle), 0,
                     -sin(angle), cos(angle), 0, 0, 0, 1), 3)
d$tensor[[1]] <- rotation %*% d$tensor[[1]] %*% t(rotation)
ggplot(d, aes(x, y, z = z, tensor = tensor, fill = shape)) +
  geom_tensor_3d(glyph = "superquadric", gamma = 3) + coord_3d(aspect = "data")
```

Kindlmann (2004), [Superquadric tensor glyphs](https://doi.org/10.2312/VisSym/VisSym04/147-154), defines the anisotropy measures and shape equations used here.
